transcript:
Interview transcript A06 — Doctoral researcher and project research assistant
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] What's your role on the project?
[Respondent] Officially I do the fieldwork. Unofficially I'm the person who sits in the community meetings and then writes the paragraph that gets cut from the report. I've counted. Four times now.
[Interviewer] On what grounds is it cut?
[Respondent] Length, usually. Sometimes 'this belongs in the appendix'. Once, quite honestly, 'we don't want to give them ammunition'. That was said in a meeting and nobody objected, including me, and I've thought about that a lot since.
[Interviewer] Tell me about the fieldwork itself.
[Respondent] Sixty-one street intercepts and nine longer interviews, over four months, at eight junctions chosen to vary by ward income and footfall. I did evenings and weekends as well because the daytime sample was retired people and parents, which is a real population but not the whole one.
[Interviewer] Did anything surprise you?
[Respondent] How few people knew there was a system. Roughly two in three had no idea the junctions had changed at all. Which reframes the whole consultation question, doesn't it — you can't consult people about a thing they don't know exists, and the consultation was advertised in the places you'd look if you already knew.
[Interviewer] What will you do with the material that gets cut?
[Respondent] Put it in the thesis, where four people will read it. I know how that sounds. I'm also, and I go back and forth on whether this is appropriate, giving the community group a plain-language summary of my own findings directly, because they gave me the data and I don't think a paywall is a good reason for them not to have it.
